sentence: A brother sinned, and the council called an elder to come and judge him, but he refused. When pressed, he came carrying a leaking basket of sand behind him, and he said that his own sins were running out behind him and he did not see them, yet he had come to judge the sins of another. The desert sayings use such enacted parables to teach the relinquishing of judgment.

The hadith are graded by the scholars into the sound, the good, and the weak, and within the sound a further distinction is drawn for traditions transmitted by so many independent chains that collusion in error is inconceivable. A ruling in law may be built upon a sound report, while a weak report is admitted, if at all, only for the encouragement of virtuous deeds and never as a basis for obligation.

An elder was asked what he did all day in the desert, and he answered that he fell down and rose again, fell down and rose again, without ceasing. The desert sayings hold no expectation of an unbroken progress; they teach instead that the spiritual life is a matter of rising once more after each fall, and that the one who keeps rising is not defeated.

The Isha Upanishad opens with the declaration that all this, whatever moves in the moving world, is to be regarded as enveloped by the Lord. The verse counsels that one should therefore enjoy what is given through renunciation and not covet the wealth of any other, for the recognition that all is pervaded by the divine transforms possession into trust and grasping into release.

In the Chandogya Upanishad the father instructs his son to dissolve salt in water and then to taste the water at its surface, its middle, and its depths, finding it salt everywhere though the salt itself is unseen. So, the father says, the subtle essence pervades all that is, and that essence is the self of all; that thou art, he tells him, and the teaching is repeated until the truth is fixed in the listening mind.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The Sikh scripture opens with the syllable that names the one reality and proceeds to call it the True Name, teaching that the divine is known and remembered through the name above all other practices. The tradition holds that the name was true before the ages, is true now, and shall be true hereafter, and the worshipper is counselled to dwell on it with every breath, for the name is the bridge between the soul and its source.

Two birds, companions always united, cling to the selfsame tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating. The Mundaka Upanishad uses this image to distinguish the individual self caught in the experience of pleasure and sorrow from the supreme self that abides as the unmoved witness, and it teaches that when the first beholds the second, its grief departs.

The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, the narrative says, as a man speaks to his friend. Among all the figures of the deliverance the lawgiver is given a unique nearness to God, and the tradition has treasured this description, reading the friendship of Moses with the Lord as the ground of his authority and as a foreshadowing of the intimacy that the scriptures hold out to the faithful.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The Islamic theologians debated whether human acts are created by God or by the human agent, and whether the believer's faith is his own or the gift of God. One school stressed the absolute power of God, holding that he creates the act and the agent merely acquires it; another stressed human responsibility, fearing that to deny it would make the divine judgment unjust. The mainstream tradition sought a middle position that preserved both.

The classical tradition affirms that God is simple, that there is in God no composition of parts, no distinction of substance and accident, no real difference between the divine essence and its existence. Whatever is said of God is said of the one undivided reality, so that the divine wisdom and the divine power and the divine goodness are not separate perfections added to the essence but the one essence considered under different names.

The discourse on the foundations of mindfulness instructs the practitioner to dwell contemplating the body in the body, the feelings in the feelings, the mind in the mind, and the mental objects in the mental objects, ardent and clearly comprehending. This, the Buddha declares, is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, and for the realisation of liberation.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The third commandment forbids taking the name of God in vain, and the tradition has read this prohibition broadly, as a guard against false oaths, against careless speech, and against any use of the name that empties it of reverence. Out of regard for the holiness of the name the later tradition substituted other words in reading aloud, so that the name might be honoured in being not pronounced.

The wisdom literature pictures the creation as the work of a divine wisdom present at the founding of the world, beside the creator as a master craftsman when he marked out the foundations of the earth and assigned the sea its limit. The cosmos, on this reading, is not a brute fact but the expression of an intelligence, and its order is the trace of the wisdom by which it was made.

When Zhuangzi was dying, his disciples wished to give him a lavish burial. He told them he would have heaven and earth for his coffin, the sun and moon for his jade ornaments, and the stars for his pearls; what funeral furnishings could be lacking? When they protested that crows would eat him, he replied that above ground the crows would eat him and below ground the ants would, and he asked why they would rob the one to feed the other.

Surdas, blind from birth, sings of the child Krishna at play in the cowherd village, stealing butter and dancing in the dust, and the poet declares that though his outward eyes are dark, the inward eye beholds the lord at every moment. The bhakti tradition cherished the songs of the divine childhood, finding in the tender scenes a love that draws the heart more surely than the contemplation of majesty.

The one who is the same to friend and foe, the same in honour and dishonour, the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, free from attachment, to whom blame and praise are equal, content with whatever comes, having no fixed abode, steady of mind and full of devotion, that person, Krishna says to Arjuna, is dear to me. The Gita draws the portrait of the soul made even by discipline.

I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. The first words of the Decalogue ground the commandments in an act of deliverance, so that the law is given not to a people newly enslaved but to one already redeemed, and obedience is asked as the response of gratitude rather than the price of freedom.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: The Word that was with God, the gospel teaches, was the light that enlightens everyone, coming into the world. The interpreters have read this verse as a teaching that the eternal Word is the source of all true illumination, present in some manner to every human being, so that the incarnation does not begin the divine self-communication but brings to a focus a light that had never been wholly absent.

The transfiguration on the mountain, where the face of Jesus shone like the sun and his garments became white as light, was read by the contemplative tradition as a glimpse of the glory that the soul is destined to share. The Eastern church in particular found in the uncreated light of the mountain a sign of the divine energies, accessible to those whose hearts have been purified by long prayer.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? The apostle's question became a cornerstone of the doctrine of grace, for the theologians read it as ruling out every claim of merit, and as teaching that even the faith by which a person receives salvation is itself a gift, so that gratitude rather than boasting is the only fitting response.

Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits, who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy. As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. The two parables press the same point: the kingdom is worth everything one has.

The scriptures record prayers of intercession in which one person stands before God on behalf of others, Abraham pleading for the city, Moses interceding for the people who had sinned, the prophet praying for those who had wronged him. The tradition has read these scenes as a teaching that prayer reaches beyond the one who prays, and that to bear another before God is among the highest forms of love.

Out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord. Lord, hear my voice; let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy. If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared. I wait for the Lord, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning.

The midrash on the binding of Isaac fills the silences of the terse biblical narrative, asking what passed between father and son on the three days of the journey, and what Abraham felt as he raised the knife. The rabbis multiply readings, some imagining the son a willing participant who asked to be bound tightly lest he flinch, and the midrash thus draws out of a few verses a meditation on faith and obedience.

The fathers read the Old Testament as a book full of Christ, finding him prefigured in the paschal lamb, in the rock that gave water in the wilderness, and in the bronze serpent lifted up by Moses. This typological reading was not, in their understanding, an arbitrary imposition, for they believed the same God authored both Testaments and so wove the earlier history with foreshadowings of the later fulfilment.

The Eastern tradition speaks of the mutual indwelling of the three persons, each wholly in the others, a coinherence so complete that to see one is to see the others and to act is to act as one. The image offered is of three lamps in a single room whose lights so interpenetrate that no beam can be assigned to one alone, and yet the lamps remain three.

From the whirlwind God answers Job not with an explanation of his suffering but with a long survey of the creation, the foundations of the earth, the storehouses of the snow, the wild ass and the eagle and the great creatures of the deep. The answer does not solve the problem on Job's terms but enlarges the frame, and Job, having glimpsed a wisdom beyond his reckoning, falls silent and is comforted.

Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice say that the dwelling place of God is with man, and that he will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

The Hindu scriptures distinguish between texts regarded as heard, the eternal revelation comprising the Vedas, and texts regarded as remembered, the vast body of tradition including the epics and the law codes. The first category is held to be authorless and beginningless, and the second derives its authority from being grounded in the first, a distinction that orders the immense literature of the tradition.

The kingdom of heaven, Jesus said, may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son and sent his servants to call those who were invited, but they would not come. So he sent his servants into the roads to invite everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests. The parable warns that the first-invited may forfeit their place and that the feast will not remain empty.

When Paul writes that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law, he is not dismissing obedience but relocating its source. Righteousness, in his argument to the Romans, is reckoned to Abraham before circumcision and before the giving of the Torah, so that the promise might rest on grace. The believer is incorporated into Christ's death and raised with him, and from this union the fruit of the Spirit follows as consequence rather than precondition.

The prayer of thanksgiving at the table recalls the whole work of salvation before it asks anything, rehearsing the creation, the covenant, and the redemption, so that the petition rests upon remembrance. Lift up your hearts, the celebrant says, and the people answer that they lift them to the Lord, and the dialogue draws the assembly into the act of giving thanks that gives the rite its name.

The Master said that at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he stood firm, at forty he had no doubts, at fifty he knew the decree of heaven, at sixty his ear was obedient, and at seventy he could follow what his heart desired without overstepping the bounds. The Analects records this account of a lifetime's growth as a measure of the moral self-cultivation the tradition holds before the learner.

The Zoroastrian tradition gathers the moral teaching into a threefold formula that the scriptures repeat as the path of the faithful: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds. The believer is called to align the inner life, the speech, and the action with truth, taking part in the great struggle between truth and falsehood that the scriptures place at the centre of the cosmos.

When God finally speaks to Job from the whirlwind, the long-awaited answer is not a defence of the divine justice but a series of questions that Job cannot answer. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades? The interpreters have read this response as a refusal of the terms of the debate, an enlargement of Job's vision rather than a verdict in his case.

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand. The prophet opens his book by summoning the cosmos as witness to a covenant lawsuit, charging the people with an ingratitude the dumb beasts do not share.

The Muslim tradition holds that the Quran was collected into a single authoritative codex within the first decades after the Prophet's death. The reciters who had preserved the revelation were consulted, the written fragments were gathered, and a standard text was established and copies sent to the major centres, while variant copies were set aside, so that the community would recite from one text.

The hymns of praise in the Psalter call the whole creation to worship, summoning the sun and moon, the sea creatures and the deeps, the mountains and the cattle, the kings of the earth and all peoples. This widening summons reflects a conviction that praise is the proper response of every creature to its maker, and that the worshipper who joins the chorus is taking up a role assigned in the order of things.

The tantric scriptures place great weight on the relationship between the teacher and the disciple, holding that the esoteric instruction cannot be received from a book alone but must be conferred through initiation. The text describes the rite by which the teacher empowers the disciple, opening the practice and binding the disciple to its vows, and it warns that the teaching pursued without this transmission is fruitless or even harmful.

The book of Job has been read across the traditions as the scripture that refuses every premature consolation, that lets the sufferer rage and question without condemning him, and that ends not with an answer to the problem of evil but with an encounter. The interpreters have held that the book's wisdom lies in this very restraint, the willingness to leave the hardest question open while affirming that the questioner is not abandoned.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The apostle's closing greeting, naming the three together in a single blessing, was treasured by the church as an early witness to the trinitarian faith, and the interpreters found in its order and its rhythm a confession woven into the texture of the apostolic letters.

The Dhammapada opens with the teaching that the mind is the forerunner of all states, that they are wrought by the mind and made of the mind. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows as the wheel follows the foot of the ox; if one speaks or acts with a serene mind, happiness follows like a shadow that never departs.

The covenant with David promises an enduring house, declaring that the king's offspring will be established after him and that his throne will be made firm forever. The prophet brings this word to David in the night, and the covenant becomes the seed of a long expectation, for when the kingdom falls the promise is remembered, and the hope of an anointed heir to David's throne is carried into the prophetic books.

Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, form is not other than emptiness. So too feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. The Heart Sutra presses this teaching to its farthest reach, declaring that in emptiness there is no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind, and finally no path, no wisdom, and no attainment, since there is nothing to be attained.

The book of Job ends by declaring that the friends have not spoken of God what is right, as Job has, and the verdict has long puzzled the interpreters, since Job said many bitter things. The traditional reading holds that Job is vindicated not for the accuracy of his words but for the honesty of his address, for speaking to God rather than merely about him, while the friends defended a doctrine and missed the man.

The Master said that the noble person understands what is right, while the small person understands what is profitable. The Analects draws this contrast repeatedly, marking the noble person not by birth or rank but by the orientation of the will, the readiness to do what is fitting even at a cost, and the tradition holds this figure before the learner as the goal of the long labour of self-cultivation.

When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus took a child and set the child among them, saying that whoever would be first must be last of all and servant of all, and that unless they turned and became like children they would not enter the kingdom. The teaching makes the lowliness of a child, who claims no rank, the very condition of entry.

The cobbler Ravidas sings that even one of low birth, despised by the proud, becomes worthy through the love of the lord, and that the name lifts the lowliest above the high-born who lack it. The bhakti poets repeatedly proclaim that devotion overturns the orders of caste and station, for the divine, they sing, regards the heart and not the rank of the worshipper.

The Islamic theologians debated whether the attributes of God, his knowledge, his power, his speech, are identical with the essence or in some way distinct from it. Some held that the attributes are neither the essence nor other than the essence, a formula meant to affirm their reality while denying any plurality of gods, and the discussion shaped the doctrine of the divine names that the tradition holds to be ninety-nine.

The scriptures join prayer to the forgiveness of others and to the setting right of wrongs, teaching that the hands lifted in prayer must be clean and that the worshipper who comes to the altar must first be reconciled with his brother. Prayer, on this teaching, is not sealed off from conduct but bound to it, and a life at odds with the neighbour cannot offer an undivided heart to God.

The scriptures describe a creation that is declared good and yet entrusted to the care of the creatures within it. The human being is set in the garden to work it and keep it, and the dominion granted is read by the interpreters as a stewardship rather than a licence, the creation order placing humanity within the world as its tender rather than above it as its owner.

Divine omniscience is held to extend not only to all actual things but to all possible things and to the free acts of creatures, and the theologians have long debated how this knowledge is compatible with freedom. Some have located the answer in the eternity of God, who sees all times at once as present, so that the divine knowledge does not foresee the free act as future but beholds it as it occurs.

The book of Deuteronomy renews the covenant on the plains of Moab for the generation about to enter the land. Choose life, the people are urged, that you and your offspring may live, loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice, and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days. The covenant is set before them as a decision, with heaven and earth called to witness.

God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. The apostolic writers quote this saying from the older scriptures and draw from it a counsel to humble oneself under the mighty hand of God, holding that the lowly heart is the one to which grace can be given, since pride closes the hand that humility opens to receive.

You shall not steal. The commandment protects the neighbour's property, and the interpreters have extended it to forbid not only theft by stealth but fraud, the withholding of wages, the use of false weights, and every gain taken at the expense of another's right. The tradition reads the commandment as a charge to deal honestly, so that the eighth word becomes the foundation of a just commerce.

Wisdom in the book of Proverbs is personified as a woman who cries aloud in the street and calls at the city gates, offering her instruction to all who will receive it. She declares that the Lord possessed her at the beginning of his work, that she was beside him as a master craftsman when he established the heavens, and that whoever finds her finds life.

A dispute is for the sake of heaven, the sages teach, if it resembles the disputes of Hillel and Shammai, and such a dispute will endure; a dispute not for the sake of heaven, like that of Korah and his company, will not endure. The distinction lies not in the agreement reached but in the motive of the disputants, for the argument pursued in the search for truth has lasting value even when it is not resolved.

The Sabbath is given as a sign of the covenant, a perpetual reminder set within the rhythm of every week. The Israelites are to keep the Sabbath throughout their generations, the text declares, as a covenant forever, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested. The covenant is thus woven into the ordering of time itself.

A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. Many of the proverbs concern the power of speech, observing that words can heal or wound, that a fitly spoken word is like apples of gold, and that even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise.

And God said to Noah, this is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. The first of the great covenants is made not with a people but with all flesh, and its sign is given in the sky for every generation to see.

The Way that can be spoken of is not the constant Way; the name that can be named is not the constant name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things. So the opening of the Daodejing sets a paradox at the head of its teaching, for it commends a reality that withdraws from every word offered to capture it.

Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, have mercy on us; grant us peace. This invocation, sung before the sharing of the bread, draws on the words by which John pointed to Jesus and turns them into a plea, repeated so that the congregation may dwell on the mercy it asks before approaching the table.

By thinking, the divine cannot be reduced to thought, even if one thinks a hundred thousand times. By remaining silent, inner silence is not obtained, even if one remains absorbed in trance. The hunger of the hungry is not satisfied, even by piling up the loads of the world. Guru Nanak asks in the Japji how then one may become true and break the wall of falsehood, and he answers that it is by walking in the will of the divine.

The second account of creation, beginning with the man formed from the dust of the ground and the breath of life breathed into his nostrils, has a different texture from the first. It moves from a dry land awaiting rain to a planted garden, and it places the human creature at the centre from the start, naming the animals and finding among them no helper fit for him until the woman is made.

The Prophet is reported to have said that whoever attributes to him a saying he did not utter should prepare a seat for himself in the fire. This warning, itself a hadith, made the fabrication of traditions a grave offence and gave urgency to the work of the critics, who held that the integrity of the prophetic record was a trust the community was bound to guard.

None of you truly believes, the Prophet is reported to have said, until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. The traditions of this kind, brief and ethical, were gathered into collections of forty hadith intended for memorisation, and teachers held that a person who preserved and acted upon such a number would be raised among the learned.

The covenant of the primordial day, in which the Quran relates that God drew forth the descendants of Adam and asked whether he was not their Lord, and they answered yes, became for the Sufi commentators the charter of the soul's longing. Every later yearning for God, they taught, is the memory of that answer, and the recitation of the verse stirs in the heart a recognition older than the present life.

Naked I came from my mother's womb, Job says when the news of his losses reaches him, and naked shall I return; the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. The book records this as the first response to catastrophe, an acceptance that the later chapters will strain and complicate but never wholly abandon, the wrestling that follows growing out of a devotion that the loss did not at once destroy.

The psalms turn the contemplation of the cosmos into praise, calling the heavens to declare the glory of God and the firmament to proclaim the work of his hands. The scripture reads the day and the night as a speech without words, a testimony poured forth through all the earth, so that the order of the creation is itself a kind of utterance addressed to whoever will attend.

When Moses came to the burning bush, the Quran relates, he was called by name and told to remove his sandals, for he stood in a sacred valley. He was shown the sign of the staff that became a serpent and the hand that shone white, and he was sent to a tyrant with the request that he loosen his tongue so that the people might understand his speech. The narrative dwells on the prophet's fear and his prayer for a helper.

The companion who reported the largest number of traditions explained that he had remained in the company of the Prophet while others were occupied with trade and farming, and that he had prayed for a memory that would not lose what it received. The scholars of hadith recorded such accounts to establish how a transmitter came by his knowledge and why his reports might be trusted.

The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. The creation narrative gives the human creature a charge from the beginning, and the words for working and keeping have been read as a teaching that labour is not a curse but a vocation set before the fall, the cultivation of the world being part of the original blessing.

Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. The words spoken from the cross have been read by the tradition as the supreme enactment of the teaching on forgiveness, the wronged one praying for the wrongdoers in the very hour of the wrong, and the interpreters have found in the plea of ignorance a model for the charity that seeks the least culpable reading of an offence.

The lights set in the firmament are appointed, the narrative says, to separate the day from the night, to be for signs and for seasons and for days and years. The interpreters have noted that the sun and moon are not named in the account but called simply the greater light and the lesser light, and they have read this reticence as a deliberate refusal to honour with names the bodies that the neighbouring peoples worshipped.

Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The book of Ecclesiastes presses the question of meaning to its limit, surveying labour, pleasure, and wisdom alike and finding each unable to secure a lasting gain.

The fourth song of the servant in the prophet describes a figure who suffers not for his own wrongdoing but for the wrongdoing of others, who is wounded for their transgressions and by whose stripes they are healed. The passage opens a possibility that the older doctrine of retribution could not hold, that suffering may be borne on behalf of the many and may itself be the means of their restoration.

The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: stand in the gate of the Lord's house and proclaim there this word. Do not trust in these deceptive words, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord. For if you truly amend your ways and your deeds, if you truly execute justice one with another, then I will let you dwell in this place. The oracle attacks the false security that treats the sanctuary as a guarantee.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: The book of Ben Sira warns repeatedly about the power of the tongue, declaring that a slip on the pavement is better than a slip of the tongue, and that many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as have fallen because of the tongue. The sage counsels the making of a balance and a scale for one's words, and the setting of a door and a bolt upon the mouth.

The apostle writes that he knew a man caught up to the third heaven, whether in the body or out of the body he could not tell, who heard things that cannot be told, which no one may utter. The mystics returned often to this passage, finding in it a warrant for an experience of God so far beyond ordinary cognition that language fails before it, and a reticence that they took as the proper response to such a gift.

The teaching on the intermediate state, the condition of the soul between death and the general resurrection, has occupied theologians who sought to reconcile the scriptures that speak of the dead as sleeping with those that promise the believer an immediate entry into the divine presence. The traditions have answered variously, but all have held that the final hope is bound to the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the whole creation.

The latter chapters of the narrative are given over to the instructions for the tabernacle, the dwelling that the people are to make so that the divine presence may go with them. The detailed prescriptions for the curtains, the ark, the lampstand, and the priestly garments have been read as a sign that the law-giving issues in worship, the covenant providing not only a code but a place of meeting.

The collect, a brief prayer that gathers the petitions of the assembly, follows a tight form: an address to God, a clause recalling some attribute or act, a single petition, an aspiration toward the fruit of the petition, and a closing that prays through Christ. The economy of the form allows it to be heard whole, and the church appoints a proper collect for each day so that the prayer is fitted to the season.

subtopic: Doctrine of grace and free will
sentence: The scriptures hold together in tension the assertion that salvation is the work of God and the call to the human will to repent and believe. Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, the apostle writes, and in the same breath adds that it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. The theologians have read this verse as a charter for affirming both the divine initiative and the human response.

An elder taught that the beginning of the soul's healing is to keep watch over the thoughts, for the deed is the fruit of the thought, and the one who lets a wandering thought grow unchecked will find it bearing him away. The desert sayings devote much attention to the discernment of thoughts, teaching the monk to recognise the suggestion at its first rising and to turn from it before it takes hold.

What is your only comfort in life and in death, the catechism of Heidelberg asks, and answers that it is that I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. The confession is cast as a personal assurance, and the question-and-answer form was designed to be learned by heart so that the doctrine would be ready in the hour of trial.

The Quran establishes the pilgrimage to the sacred house as a duty upon those who are able to make the journey, and it traces the rite to Abraham, who is said to have raised the foundations of the house and to have been commanded to proclaim the pilgrimage among the people. The pilgrim, entering the state of consecration, sets aside the ordinary garments and the ordinary concerns and turns wholly toward the rite.

The kingdom of heaven, the parable runs, is like a net thrown into the sea that gathered fish of every kind. When it was full the fishermen drew it ashore and sorted the good into containers and threw away the bad. So it will be at the close of the age, Jesus said, when the angels will separate the evil from the righteous. The parable, like that of the weeds, defers the sorting to the end.

Augustine, expounding the opening of Genesis, warned that the interpreter must not cling so firmly to a particular reading of the literal sense that, when fuller knowledge corrects it, the faith itself is brought into disrepute. He held that scripture accommodates itself to the capacities of its readers, and that where the letter seems to teach what is unworthy of God, the spiritual sense must be sought.

Abraham is presented in the Quran as the friend of God who broke with the idols of his people. He questioned the worship of the stars and the sun and the moon, observing that what set could not be his Lord, and he confronted his father and his community, asking what they worshipped and whether the carved images could hear them or do them good or harm. The narrative makes him the model of pure devotion to the one God.

Augustine, seeking analogies for the Trinity, looked into the structure of the human mind and found there a likeness in the mind that knows itself and loves itself, three and yet one. He offered the analogy with caution, knowing that no creature can fully image the creator, but he held that the soul, made in the divine image, bears some trace of the triune life of the God who made it.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. The gospel's prologue moves from the eternal Word to the incarnation in a single sentence, and the verb rendered dwelt has been read as an echo of the tabernacle, the Word pitching his tent among a people as the divine presence once filled the sanctuary.

The Katha Upanishad sets the teaching of immortality in a dialogue between the boy Nachiketa and Death himself. Death offers wealth and long life and the pleasures of the world, but the boy refuses them all, asking only to know what lies beyond death. The teaching that follows compares the self to the rider of a chariot, the body to the chariot, the intellect to the charioteer, and the senses to the horses that must be governed.

The prophet Hosea casts the broken covenant as a marriage betrayed, and the oracle of judgment is shot through with the language of a wounded love. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, the prophet declares, and no knowledge of God in the land; there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery. Yet within the same book the judgment is interrupted by the cry of a God who asks how he can give up his people.

The Daodejing warns the ruler against governing through cleverness and law, for the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become; the sharper the weapons, the more disordered the state. It commends instead a government so light that the people scarcely know their ruler exists, and it teaches that the sage rules best who empties the people of restless ambition and fills them with what sustains.

The chariot that Ezekiel beheld by the river, the wheels within wheels, the living creatures, the gleaming throne above the firmament, became in the Jewish mystical tradition the central object of contemplation. The discipline that grew around this vision was guarded with care, for the sages held that the work of the chariot should not be expounded except to one who is wise and understands of his own knowledge.

Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. The command grounds its demand in the character of God, whose generosity does not discriminate, and it asks the disciple to imitate that indiscriminate love.

Therefore do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. The sermon counsels a freedom from anxiety grounded in trust, urging that the disciple seek first the kingdom and let each day's trouble be sufficient for the day.

The Zoroastrian scriptures present the wise Lord as the creator of truth and the source of the good mind, and they place over against him the lie and the destructive spirit. The Gathas frame human life as a choice between the two ways, and they teach that each soul, by its thoughts and words and deeds, takes its side in a conflict whose outcome is the renewal of the world.

The Rule legislates for the reception of guests, instructing that all who arrive be welcomed as Christ himself, for he will say that he was a stranger and was taken in. The guest is to be met with prayer and the kiss of peace, and proper honour is to be shown especially to the poor and to pilgrims, since in the rich the awe they inspire already secures their welcome.

A young monk asked an elder why, though he prayed, his heart remained dry. The old man said that the water wears away the stone not by its force but by its constancy, drop after drop, and that so the soul is softened not by a single great prayer but by the patient repetition of the small ones. The desert sayings teach perseverance over intensity.

The Buddhist tradition does not possess a single closed canon, for the scriptures were preserved in several languages and several collections. The Pali canon, organised into three baskets of discipline, discourses, and higher teaching, is held authoritative by one branch, while other branches received a wider body of sutras, and the question of which texts are the genuine word of the Buddha has been answered differently across the schools.

The Lankavatara Sutra warns against grasping emptiness as a thing in itself, calling those who do so incurable. Emptiness, it teaches, is not a void to be apprehended but the absence of the imagined self-nature that the deluded mind projects onto experience. The remedy for clinging to existence is the teaching of emptiness, but one who then clings to emptiness has fallen into a subtler error.

Mirabai sings that she has taken the dark lord for her husband and will have no other, that she has danced before the world and let her good name fall, for the love of the divine has made her careless of what people say. The devotional verse of the bhakti poets often speaks in the voice of the beloved, casting the soul's longing for God in the language of an all-consuming human love.

The tension between James and Paul on faith and works has occupied commentators for centuries. James insists that faith without works is dead, citing the same Abraham whom Paul makes the model of believing trust. Many resolve the apparent contradiction by noting that the two writers use the word works differently: Paul opposes works of the law as a boundary marker of covenant membership, while James condemns a barren profession that produces no love of neighbour.

The midrashic reading often connects a verse from one part of the scripture with a distant verse from another, drawing them together by a shared word so that each illumines the other. This technique treats the whole of the scripture as a single fabric, and the rabbis held that a verse in the law might be unlocked by a phrase in the psalms, since one author, in their belief, had woven the whole.

In the garden before his death, the gospel records, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from him, and then added the words, yet not what I will, but what you will. The tradition has read this prayer as the pattern of all petition, the honest naming of the desire of the heart held within a final surrender to the will of God, so that prayer asks freely and yet entrusts the outcome.

The interpreters have long pondered why the scriptures open with two creation accounts that differ in order and emphasis, the first placing the human creature last and the second placing him first. The traditional reading holds that the two are complementary rather than contradictory, the first surveying the cosmic order and the second drawing near to the human story that the rest of the book will tell.

The Quran recounts the trial of Abraham, who saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son, and who told the boy of the vision. The son answered that his father should do as he was commanded and would find him, God willing, among the patient. When both had submitted and the father had laid the son down, a voice called out that he had fulfilled the dream, and a great sacrifice was given in the boy's place.

Praise the Lord! Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens. Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to his excellent greatness. Praise him with trumpet sound; praise him with lute and harp. Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. The final psalm closes the Psalter with an unbroken summons to praise, naming the instruments and ending with the whole of breathing creation.

The teaching on the inward law intensifies the commandments rather than relaxing them. It is not enough not to murder, for anyone who is angry with his brother is liable to judgment; it is not enough not to commit adultery, for everyone who looks with lustful intent has already committed it in his heart. The sermon locates moral failure in the disposition and not only in the deed.

The Acaranga Sutra, among the oldest of the Jain texts, preserves the discipline of the wandering monk in spare and severe prose. It teaches that the one who knows the nature of harm knows the nature of restraint, and it describes the ascetic who endures heat and cold, hunger and the abuse of others, without complaint, for the scriptures hold that equanimity under hardship purifies the soul of its bondage.

The theologians distinguish the persons of the Trinity by their relations of origin, the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten of the Father, the Spirit proceeding. These relations, they teach, do not divide the one essence but subsist within it, so that what distinguishes the persons is precisely their relation to one another, and the divine unity is not threatened by the distinction.

The Vedic scriptures place the sacrifice at the centre of the cosmic order, and the hymn of the cosmic person describes the world itself as fashioned from the offering of a primal being. The ritual fire, fed with the prescribed oblations and accompanied by the appointed verses, was held to sustain the order of the seasons and the gods, so that the sacrifice was understood as a participation in the maintenance of the world.

And all the people answered together and said, all that the Lord has spoken we will do. The narrative records the people's assent before the full body of the law has been given, and the interpreters have read this as a teaching that the covenant is entered by trust, the people binding themselves to obedience in advance, on the strength of the deliverance already received.

A brother asked an elder for a word of salvation, and the old man was silent a long while, then said only that he should forgive his neighbour, and the neighbour would be forgiven, and so the brother himself would be forgiven. The desert sayings, for all the severity of their askesis, return again and again to this simple root, that the gate of mercy opens for the one who has opened it for another.

The Master said that he transmitted but did not create, that he trusted in and loved the ancients. The Analects presents the teacher not as the founder of a new doctrine but as the faithful conveyor of an inherited wisdom, and the classics that the tradition gathered, the odes, the documents, the rites, and the changes, were valued as the deposit of that ancient teaching to be studied and handed on.

The phrase of one substance with the Father was the decisive word at Nicaea, chosen because it could not be evaded by those who wished to call the Son divine in a lesser sense. Its critics objected that the term was not found in scripture, and the defenders replied that no single word of scripture could be set against the heretical reading, so that a precise term was needed to guard the biblical confession.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: Before Abraham was, Jesus says in the gospel, I am. The hearers take up stones, understanding the words as a claim that could not be made by a creature, and the gospel records the saying as one of the sharpest expressions of its Christology, the bare verb of being set against the long ages of the patriarch, an assertion of existence that knows no beginning.

You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. The commandment, set in the first instance against perjury in a court, has been read by the tradition more broadly as a guard upon truthful speech, forbidding slander, the spreading of rumour, and the silence that lets a falsehood stand. The neighbour's good name, the interpreters teach, is entrusted to the keeping of all who speak of him.

The weaver Kabir sings that the lord is not in the temple nor in the mosque, not in the pilgrimage nor in the fasting, but is found in the breath of the one who seeks, nearer than the seeker's own hands and feet. His verses chide both the priest and the ascetic and call the listener to a simple, inward devotion that needs no outward sign.

The vision of Isaiah in the temple, in which the prophet sees the Lord high and lifted up and the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy, was read by the contemplative tradition as a pattern of the soul's encounter with the divine majesty. The prophet's cry that he is undone, a man of unclean lips, and the burning coal that touches and purges his mouth, were taken as a figure of the purification that precedes any true ascent.

Holy God, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, have mercy on us. This ancient invocation, sung in the liturgies of the Eastern church, addresses the divine holiness three times and answers it with a plea for mercy, and the tradition surrounds it with accounts of its origin so that the congregation receives it as a prayer given rather than composed.

He has told you, O man, what is good, and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God. The prophet places humility at the close of his summary of the divine requirement, and the interpreters have read the walking humbly as the inward disposition without which the doing of justice and the loving of kindness lose their root.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest. Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. The psalm moves from the cry of abandonment to the memory of past deliverance.

The gospels present the suffering of Jesus not as a defeat to be explained away but as the centre of the story, the way by which the saving work is accomplished. The teaching that the disciple must take up the cross and follow draws the suffering of the faithful into this pattern, holding that the path of discipleship runs through hardship and that the cross is not the contradiction of the way but its very shape.

The covenant theme runs through the whole of the Hebrew scriptures as the framework of the relationship between God and Israel, and the prophets measure the people against its terms. When they denounce the nation they speak as prosecutors in a covenant lawsuit, and when they comfort it they recall the covenant's promises, so that the same bond grounds both the judgment and the hope.

The poet asks the lord why he hides, why he lets the devotee call and call and gives no sign, and then answers his own complaint, saying that the hiding is itself a grace, for it deepens the longing and makes the soul cry out the more. The bhakti verses dwell often on the pain of separation, treating the ache of the absent beloved as a fire that purifies the heart.

subtopic: Wisdom of Sirach and Ben Sira
sentence: My child, the sage writes, if you come forward to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing. Set your heart right and be steadfast, and do not be impetuous in time of calamity. Cling to him and do not depart, that you may be honoured at the end of your life. The book of Ben Sira counsels the one who would be faithful to expect trial and to hold fast through it, promising that the testing refines rather than destroys.

When you pray, the teaching instructs, do not heap up empty phrases as the pagans do, who think they will be heard for their many words; for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. The instruction frees the one who prays from the anxiety of eloquence, holding that prayer is not the persuading of a reluctant power but the address of a child to a father who already knows.

Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you. The commentators have noted that this commandment, standing between the duties toward God and the duties toward the neighbour, is the only one of the ten that carries a promise, and they have read the honour due to parents as the first form of the reverence that society depends upon.

The Buddha, in the discourse to the Kalamas, told them not to accept a teaching merely because it is handed down by tradition, or because it is found in scripture, or because it accords with reason, or out of respect for a teacher. When you know for yourselves, he said, that these things are wholesome and blameless and praised by the wise, and when undertaken lead to welfare and happiness, then you should enter upon them.

The book of Revelation ends its vision of the last things with the abolition of death itself, declaring that death and the grave are thrown into the lake of fire, and that in the renewed creation death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain. The eschatology of the New Testament thus reaches its term not in the survival of the soul but in the undoing of death.

In the discourse on loving-kindness the practitioner is instructed to radiate a boundless heart toward all beings, above, below, and across, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. Just as a mother would protect with her life her only child, so should one cultivate a limitless heart toward all living beings, and this, the discourse declares, is called the sublime abiding.

The doctrine of the Trinity arose, the theologians have held, not from speculation but from the church's effort to be faithful to its scriptures and its worship at once. The scriptures called the Father God, called the Son God, called the Spirit God, and yet confessed one God, and the worship of the church addressed the three; the doctrine is the church's attempt to hold all that it had received without surrendering any part.

The rabbis taught that the Torah has seventy faces, meaning that a single verse yields many true interpretations, and they delighted in finding in the smallest features of the text, an unusual spelling, a repeated word, a particle that seems superfluous, an opening for instruction. Nothing in the scripture, they held, is without purpose, and the diligent reader is rewarded with meanings hidden in the letters.

subtopic: Christology in the Gospel of John
sentence: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was not anything made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The opening of the gospel sets the figure of Jesus within the eternal life of God and the work of creation before it tells a single event of his earthly story.

The tradition has divided the ten commandments into two tables, the first concerning the duties owed to God and the second the duties owed to the neighbour. When Jesus was asked for the greatest commandment, he named the love of God with all the heart and the love of the neighbour as oneself, and the church has read his answer as the summary of the two tables, the whole law hanging upon these two.

Among the last words of the Buddha recorded in the discourse on the great passing away is the exhortation that all conditioned things are subject to decay, and that the disciples should strive on with diligence. The discourse relates that he had told them the teaching openly, withholding nothing in the closed fist of a teacher, and that they should henceforth be islands unto themselves, with the teaching as their refuge.

The highest good is like water, the Daodejing teaches, for water benefits the ten thousand things and does not contend, dwelling in places that people disdain. Therefore it is close to the Way. The classic repeatedly commends the yielding, the low, and the soft, holding that what is supple overcomes what is rigid and that the sage who does not strive is the one who cannot be opposed.

The recognition of a canon carried with it the conviction that revelation, in some decisive sense, was complete, and that the community would thereafter live by interpreting the received books rather than by adding to them. This belief gave the canon its function as a boundary, a fixed measure against which later teaching could be tested, and the very word for canon means a rule or measuring rod.

Elijah at the mountain of God did not find the Lord in the great wind, nor in the earthquake, nor in the fire, but in a sound of sheer silence. The mystics treasured this passage, reading the still small voice as a teaching that the divine presence is met not in the spectacular but in a stillness so deep that the soul must itself fall silent to perceive it.

An old man said that if a person held the remembrance of death always before his eyes, he would never sin, for the awareness of the brief and uncertain span would burn away the heedlessness in which wrongdoing grows. The desert sayings counsel this remembrance not as a morbid dwelling on mortality but as a discipline that gives weight and seriousness to each passing hour.

The Buddhist monastic code, the Vinaya, sets out the rules by which the community of monks orders its life, and the tradition holds that each rule was laid down by the Buddha in response to a particular occasion of misconduct. The most serious offences entail expulsion from the order, while lesser faults require confession before the assembled community, which gathers on the days of the new and full moon to recite the code in full.

When Jesus had washed the feet of his disciples, an office belonging to a servant, he said that he had given them an example, that they also should do as he had done. The scene has been read by the tradition as the enacted teaching of humility, the master taking the lowest place so that the disciples might learn that greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

The Guru Granth Sahib gathers the compositions not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of saints from beyond the Sikh community, including the weaver Kabir and the cobbler Ravidas, whose hymns sit within the scripture on the same footing as the Gurus' own. This inclusion expresses the conviction that the divine word may be uttered through any sincere devotee, regardless of caste or creed, and that truth is not the possession of one tradition.

The tantric scriptures employ a deliberately veiled language, sometimes called the twilight language, in which words carry a hidden sense beyond their surface meaning. The text warns that the uninitiated reader who takes the words literally will misunderstand them entirely, and that the true import is disclosed only by the teacher, so that the secrecy is woven into the very wording of the texts.

The story of Mary in the Quran tells how she withdrew from her people and how the angel announced to her a pure son, and she asked how she could have a son when no man had touched her. The infant Jesus, the Quran relates, spoke from the cradle in her defence, declaring himself a servant of God to whom the scripture had been given and the prophethood appointed.

On the verse that God created the great sea creatures, a midrash records the saying that this refers to the leviathan and its mate, and it weaves a tale of the taming of these creatures lest they overrun the world. The rabbis used such expansions not as mere fancy but to convey teachings about divine providence and the order set upon the powers of chaos.

subtopic: Names and attributes of the divine
sentence: The scriptures of the Hindu tradition delight in the litany of divine names, and the practice of reciting the thousand names of the deity is held to be a discipline of devotion in its own right. Each name in such a litany is a meditation, naming the divine as the support of the worlds, the abode of all beings, the imperishable, the formless and the all-formed, so that the recitation carries the mind through the whole sweep of the divine being.
